newsitem.title: JAPAN: DLR INCHES UP BY LATE TOKYO BUT ACTIVITY DULL.
newsitem.headline: DLR INCHES UP BY LATE TOKYO BUT ACTIVITY DULL.

text.p: 0637 GMT TRADED HIGH/LOW AS OF 0600 GMT

The dollar inched up against the yen and mark on short-covering by late Tokyo on Thursday, but trade remained confined to a narrow range, as players were away for the "Obon" summer holidays, dealers said.
The dollar's downside was solid near 115.50 yen on talk of steady bids from Japanese investors near 115.30 yen.
"Along with overseas players, traders who confirmed the dollar's solid floor during Tokyo trade began covering their short-positions," a dealer at a city bank said.
A dealer at a European bank said U.S. securities houses were behind the dollar purchases in late trade. He added that stop-loss purchases were triggered near 115.90 yen, pushing the greenback higher.

While trade was dominated by interbank dealers and day traders, Japanese life insurers and investment trust firms were said to be placing bids against the yen, providing firm support to the dollar, dealers said.
The mark/yen rate came under the spotlight as trade in the dollar/yen and dollar/mark was dull and lacked incentives due to the summer holidays.

The mark managed to stand above 63 yen in late Tokyo after erasing earlier losses. Offers from exporters, possibly from Japanese car makers, around 63.30-50 yen limited the mark's earlier ascent. The mark earlier rose on purchases by U.S. fund operators, dealers said. There was talk that Swiss operators were selling on rallies.
The German unit was traded at around 63.09/12 yen at 0655 GMT, compared with 63.07 yen in late New York on Wednesday.
Tokyo dealers were trying to figure out whether the dollar's recent fall against the mark was a short-term correction or a start of a long-term downward trend.

"I think that U.S. economy is still growing without inflationary pressures and overall sentiment towards the dollar remains unchanged," a city bank dealer said. He said the dollar will be well-supported despite possible further sales.

But a senior dealer at a city bank said: "Technical sentiment for the dollar/mark is deteriorating following recent falls. The dollar is likely to test the downside and a fall below 1.82 marks could trigger heavy stop-loss sales."
Dealers said another downside test for the dollar against the yen is possible in the near term if Japan's customs-cleared trade data for July, due out on Monday, shows a sharp rise.
A Reuters poll of economists produced an average forecast of an 83 percent rise in Japan's trade surplus from a year ago.
Forecasts ranged from a 60 percent to a 114 percent increase in the July surplus, or a surplus of 799 billion yen to 1.07 trillion yen.
The dollar closed at 115.70/75 yen and 1.8345/55 marks in New York on Wednesday.
